title: Motherhood in the Trenches: What Do We Owe Postpartum Women?
gist: IFS research fellow Amber Lapp uses her own severe postpartum breakdown after a fifth and sixth child — sleeplessness, rage, intrusive imagery, a tentative rapid-cycling bipolar 2 diagnosis, and neuropsych results that never came back — to argue that maternal postpartum care is scientifically thin and operationally broken. Her prescription is rest-first care, educated fathers, insurance-covered marital counseling, and houses of hospitality built on pro-life and church infrastructure, framed as the precondition for any pronatalist society.

themes.theme: Postpartum as an under-mapped clinical territory

insights.claim: The postpartum period is treated as concrete and unavoidable yet remains scientifically mysterious, with symptoms often dismissed as psychological artifacts that will clear once the fog of birth lifts.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: A large, recurring, poorly-served clinical population is the classic setup for a new care category.
insights.quote: We often treat postpartum symptoms as if they are in a woman’s mind, something that will clear up once the fog of birth lifts.
insights.locator: Motherhood is forged in the intensity

insights.claim: Postpartum crises can surface only at a specific birth rather than all of them, and can return long after the standard window — here, severe symptoms reappeared when the baby was already a year old.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Screening protocols keyed to the first weeks after birth will systematically miss late-onset and recurrent cases.
insights.locator: But just when I thought I was out of the woods

insights.claim: Diagnosis in the postpartum window is genuinely ambiguous: a well-regarded institution said the author met criteria for rapid cycling bipolar 2 but hedged that it might be a postpartum issue that would resolve with time.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Diagnostic ambiguity means mistreatment risk in both directions — an opening for better longitudinal assessment tools.
insights.locator: So I went for psychiatric evaluation

insights.claim: Sleep deprivation is identified as the load-bearing mechanism of postpartum breakdown, producing intrusive visual imagery, racing heart, sweaty palms and clenched fists over multiple sleepless days.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: If sleep is the mechanism, sleep restoration — not medication — is the highest-leverage first intervention to build services around.

insights.claim: Therapist and psychiatrist turnover forced the author to retell the darkest episode of her life to a new note-taking stranger at each visit, producing a flatline clinical response and no relief.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Continuity of care is the failure point in behavioral health — a concrete product gap for care-coordination services.
insights.quote: I left feeling like I’d gone to confession, but without the relief of absolution.
insights.locator: Gaps in Maternal Care Erode Trust

insights.claim: After completing a full battery of neuropsychological testing, the author never received results despite following up directly with the psychiatrist — and notes she would have been abandoned had she been in actual crisis.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Unreturned results are a visible quality and liability failure in a demand-overloaded system; measurable follow-up is a differentiator.
insights.locator: A few weeks later, there was still no response

insights.claim: The maternal mental health system is overloaded by high demand and even professionals appear mystified by the postpartum period and uncertain what to do.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Supply-constrained plus knowledge-constrained is where non-clinical, lower-cost respite models can legitimately take share.
insights.locator: The system is overloaded by high demand

insights.claim: Clinical appointments can be less restorative than plain rest: the author wondered whether a coffee shop with a book would have been more healing than the testing regimen she arranged a babysitter to attend.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Suggests measuring maternal interventions against a rest baseline, which most clinical pathways never test against.
insights.locator: Again, I was met by a different psychiatrist

themes.theme: Mothers and soldiers: reframing maternal sacrifice

insights.claim: The historical comparison of mothers to soldiers is revived as an analytic frame — both serve the common good sacrificially, and Theodore Roosevelt told the 1908 Congress of Mothers he ranked mothers even ahead of Civil War veterans.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: A rhetorical frame with historical precedent for large-scale material support — the language pronatal policy advocates are likely to reach for.
insights.quote: the mother is the one supreme asset of national life

insights.claim: Early twentieth-century maternalist rhetoric was both culturally ubiquitous and matched by material support, unlike today where the rhetoric persists without the resources.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Identifies the gap between pronatal talk and pronatal spending — the space where new policy proposals will land.
insights.quote: Unlike today, this early twentieth-century maternalist rhetoric was culturally ubiquitous and matched by material support.

insights.claim: Sleep insufficiency is a key driver of psychiatric symptoms in military personnel, and both veterans and postpartum mothers face heightened suicide risk — a shared physiological pathway rather than a metaphor.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: If the mechanism is shared, interventions validated in military populations could transfer directly to postpartum care.

insights.claim: The author draws an explicit kinship between postpartum breakdown and male deaths of despair, calling it the 'solidarity of the shaken' after Czech philosopher Jan Patocka.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Links two normally separate social-crisis narratives — maternal and male despair — into a single framing that broadens the coalition.
insights.quote: I feel a sort of kinship—the “solidarity of the shaken” that Czech philosopher Jan Patočka once described.

insights.claim: Well-intentioned pressure on mothers comes from two opposing directions — the career-minded, who equate contribution with paid work, and the attachment theorists, who demand total presence — and both feed the sense of being overwhelmed.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: A clean two-axis model of maternal burnout that explains why single-sided fixes (more childcare, or more leave) keep underdelivering.
insights.quote: Well-intentioned pressure on moms comes from two different fronts: the career-minded and the attachment-theorists.

insights.claim: The prescription is to prioritize motherhood without being consumed by it: a priest who counsels many mothers facing identity crises after children leave home urged the author to keep her other callings rather than cut everything else.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Empty-nest identity crisis is a downstream, decades-later cost of total-immersion parenting — an under-discussed long-horizon risk.
insights.locator: My priest friend gently encouraged me

insights.claim: Support networks are necessary but not sufficient: even with a thick web of loving people, the author could not bring herself to ask for rest, wishing instead that she were dying so she would have an excuse to lie in a hospital bed and sleep.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Demand for help does not surface voluntarily — services must be pushed and normalized rather than offered on request.
insights.quote: Even though I have a thick web of loving people in my life, there were moments when I felt desperate for rest but could not bring myself to ask for it.

insights.claim: Periodic short trips away every few months — for a friend visit, reading, writing or retreat — functioned as a reality check that restored gratitude and delight in her children on return.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: A cheap, repeatable intervention with a plausible mechanism, easier to scale than clinical treatment.

insights.claim: Charlotte Mason warned over a hundred years ago that 'the break-downs of mothers' were growing more frequent every day, indicating maternal breakdown is a recurring historical phenomenon rather than a modern novelty.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Historical recurrence argues against explanations that blame only contemporary factors like smartphones or modern work.
insights.locator: Everyone needs rest and opportunities for lifelong learning

themes.theme: Build-out proposals: rest, dads, and houses of hospitality

insights.claim: The proposed first-line treatment for mothers in crisis is rest rather than trial-and-error prescriptions and rounds of appointments — family or friends absorbing older children and practical needs so the mother does nothing but sleep, eat and care for the baby.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: A concrete, cheap alternative care pathway that competes with the psychiatric route on both cost and speed.
insights.quote: What if instead of trial-and-error prescriptions and rounds of appointments, our first course of action for mothers in crisis was simply an opportunity for rest?

insights.claim: Fathers of postpartum mothers are themselves destabilized and undertrained — sometimes heroic, sometimes shutting down — so educating dads on the postpartum period and its red flags is proposed as a distinct intervention.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Expands the postpartum service market from mother-only to couple-level products.

insights.claim: Making it a norm for insurance to cover marital counseling in the early years after birth is proposed as a concrete payer-side reform for couples under postpartum stress.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: An explicit reimbursement ask — watch whether payers or state mandates pick it up, which would create a funded market overnight.

insights.claim: The author imagines houses of hospitality for new mothers — homey and welcoming like birthing centers, for mothers not yet in full psychiatric crisis but needing respite — as a missing tier of care.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Defines a missing middle between doing nothing and psychiatric admission — the tier where new facility models usually get built.

insights.claim: The pro-life movement's existing network of women's centers, plus houses of worship whose buildings sit underutilized midweek, are identified as the ready-made infrastructure for postpartum respite care.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Repurposing existing real estate and volunteer networks is the lowest-capital path to scaling this care tier.
insights.locator: Maybe this is something that the pro-life movement

insights.claim: Answering what mothers are owed after birth is framed as the precondition for a pronatalist society, tying postpartum care directly to fertility policy.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Connects maternal mental health spending to the fertility agenda, which is where political energy and funding currently sit.
insights.quote: If we fail to provide an answer, we fail to lay the foundation required for a pronatalist society.
insights.locator: What are mothers due in the months after giving birth?

insights.claim: Pro-family conservatives are urged not to fear discussing the complexities of women's postpartum health, with dedicated study of what helps postpartum mothers thrive positioned as giving real life to the pronatalist vision.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: Signals a coalition shift: maternal mental health research gaining a right-of-center constituency broadens its funding base.
insights.quote: Pro-family conservatives need not fear discussing the complexities of women’s postpartum health.

insights.claim: The public debate is anchored to the recent Lindsay Clancy mistrial and its divided public response, which is what forced reconsideration of postpartum obligations.
insights.speaker: Amber Lapp
insights.so_what: A live legal catalyst keeping postpartum psychiatric care in the news — the kind of event that moves policy windows.
insights.locator: But the Lindsay Clancy case has forced me
